{"id": "96:17/q03", "question": "What rhetorical force does the imperative and its fāʾ carry?", "turns_on": "The notes vary in whether the taunt stresses his failure to act, the impotence of his group, or the ironic claim of noble defenders.", "positions": [{"id": "96:17/q03/p1", "position": "It is a taunting challenge that exposes his inability to summon effective help.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān says God will not enable him and angels would seize him openly; al-Ālūsī quotes this and Ibn ʿĀshūr says 96:19's kallā confirms he will not carry it out. {"id": "96:17/q04", "question": "How is the command read in the reported variant?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "96:17/q04/p1", "position": "The reading attributed to Ibn Masʿūd says to call to his council and changes the following response to 'then I will call'.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ reports ʿAbd Allāh's reading with ilā before nādiyah and fa-sa-adʿū for the answering call; Ibn ʿAṭiyya independently reports Ibn Masʿūd's 'to his council'."}]}
{"id": "96:17/q05", "question": "Who or what is his nādī?", "turns_on": "Whether the term denotes the present assembly and its people, a specifically named social body or companion, or a symbolic inward resource; the lexical notes also distinguish consultation from generosity associations.", "positions": [{"id": "96:17/q05/p1", "position": "It is the people of his gathering, his companions, supporters, clan or wider faction whom he expects to help.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ says Arabs name a man's group by council, assembly, gathering or witness, and cites a poet. Abū ʿUbayda, Ibn Hishām and others distinguish the venue from its people: the place bears the name while they meet there. Ibn Hishām cites 29:29, 19:73, 12:82 and verses by ʿUbayd, Salama and al-Kumayt. Jarīr, Zuhayr and an unnamed poet supply council and station parallels; Abū Ḥayyān observes Jarīr's adjectives describe attendees, not masonry. Muʾarrij gives Quraysh usage; Ibn ʿĀshūr notes a daytime gathering, unlike night sāmir (23:67). Bint al-Shāṭiʾ cites 68:21, 40:32, 29:29 and 19:73 for related root uses. Elmalılı compares an assembly, congress or parliament and proposes Turkish kurultay. Al-Iṣlāḥī says a linked communal group or party. The cited poetic wording and attribution vary, including Jarīr versus Dhū al-Rumma."}, {"id": "96:17/q05/p2", "position": "Specifically, his supporters are Banū Makhzūm.", "reasons": "Muqātil names the clan behind Abū Jahl's gathering."}, {"id": "96:17/q05/p3", "position": "It is an individual companion or fellow sitter.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports this as an alternative to the gathered council or its people."}, {"id": "96:17/q05/p4", "position": "Historically it is Mecca's pagan elders' council, Dār al-Nadwah.", "reasons": "Asad reports this as the classical historical identification; al-Rāzī invokes Dār al-Nadwah as evidence of consultation usage. Ibn ʿĀshūr says Quṣayy founded its council house by the Sacred Mosque for affairs, contracts and puberty ceremonies; he traces later purchases and mosque incorporation, while Bursawī notes its later Hanafi gathering hall."}, {"id": "96:17/q05/p5", "position": "In the deeper general reading, his 'council' is the arrogance that makes humans imagine they are self-sufficient.", "reasons": "Asad prefers this from the language of 96:6–7 over the historical council reading."}, {"id": "96:17/q05/p6", "position": "The word can evoke a gathering marked by generosity or hospitality.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī associates the place with generosity and hospitality; al-Rāzī reports a generosity derivation and says it makes Abū Jahl's appeal to supposed noble defenders sarcastic."}]}

{"id": "96:17/q07", "question": "Why is the gathering called 'his'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "96:17/q07/p1", "position": "It is attached to Abū Jahl because he is its chief and its members gather around him.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr cites an Arab woman's praise of a man as master of his council and support for those in need; his boast treats followers as proof of leadership."}]}
{"id": "96:17/q08", "question": "What did the reports say prompted this challenge?", "turns_on": "The reports differ in the threat, the visual barrier or angelic intervention, the order of boast and recitation, and whether a scene or grading is preserved.", "positions": [{"id": "96:17/q08/p1", "position": "Abū Jahl barred the praying Prophet, boasted of the valley's largest gathering, and the verses answered his boast.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās places the confrontation at the Maqām and says angels would seize him if he summoned his group; al-Tirmidhī's grading is given as ḥasan gharīb ṣaḥīḥ by al-Qurṭubī and ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ by Ibn Kathīr and al-Suyūṭī. Reports vary over whether the Prophet's rebuke is preserved, whether the boasts follow recitation, and whether his threat is explicit. The Prophet says the space between them darkened or that he saw ranks; variants specify the prayer place and whether the revealed sequence included 96:1."}, {"id": "96:17/q08/p4", "position": "When Abū Jahl moved toward the praying Prophet, he recoiled from a trench of fire, terror and wings; angels would have torn him limb from limb.", "reasons": "Abū Hurayra transmits the scene; al-Ṭabarī notes uncertainty over attribution of the quoted revelation. {"id": "96:17/q09", "question": "When is the threatened seizure or defeat realized?", "turns_on": "Whether the angels' seizure is the immediate counter to his call, a Badr fulfillment, or an afterlife punishment.", "positions": [{"id": "96:17/q09/p1", "position": "If he summoned his group or approached, the angels would seize him immediately, visibly.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās repeatedly gives this conditional explanation, and the Prophet's warning in the trample reports is similar. {"id": "96:17/q10", "question": "How does this challenge connect to the surrounding verses?", "turns_on": "The connection may stress the counter-summons of 96:18 or the broader self-sufficiency theme of 96:6–7 and denial in 96:19.", "positions": [{"id": "96:17/q10/p1", "position": "His call to a human council is met by God's call to the zabāniya, exposing the council's helplessness.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, al-Rāzī and Ibn Kathīr relate 96:17 to 96:18. {"id": "96:17/q11", "question": "What broader lesson is drawn from this challenge?", "turns_on": "The sources differ between a lesson directly drawn from calling the council and a broader contrast of worldly pursuit with knowledge.", "positions": [{"id": "96:17/q11/p1", "position": "Worldly status, clan and companions can embolden arrogance but cannot protect the transgressor against God.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says disbelievers rely on community for pride and fear becoming followers; Quṭb and Bint al-Shāṭiʾ describe the same illusion of family protection. {"id": "96:18/q01", "question": "How is 'We will summon' read?", "turns_on": "The verb's agent and voice, and the wording of the preceding challenge.", "positions": [{"id": "96:18/q01/p1", "position": "The common reading has active first-person plural sanadʿu: God summons the zabāniya.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān calls this the majority reading; al-Samīn calls the plural majestic. {"id": "96:18/q02", "question": "What is the grammatical mood of sanadʿu?", "turns_on": "Whether the preceding imperative governs God's answering verb.", "positions": [{"id": "96:18/q02/p1", "position": "It is indicative: no subjunctive or jussive governor precedes it.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī rejects the proposed jussive response to the command as weak; he and his full version note the independent clause."}, {"id": "96:18/q02/p2", "position": "It is jussive as the answer to the taunting command to summon the council.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the challenged man's summons is answered by God's counter-summons, and the future prefix strengthens the response."}]}
{"id": "96:18/q03", "question": "Why does the muṣḥaf write sanadʿu without its final wāw?", "turns_on": "Whether the spelling reflects pronunciation, economy, rhetorical force, or the pause form.", "positions": [{"id": "96:18/q03/p1", "position": "The spelling follows loss of wāw in connected pronunciation before a quiescent consonant.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ cites yadʿu al-insān and three poetic parallels; Abū Ḥayyān, Ibn Khālawayh as quoted by Bursawī, al-Ālūsī and Ibn ʿĀshūr explain the meeting of two vowelless letters. Ibn ʿĀshūr notes it is no verse-end pause."}, {"id": "96:18/q03/p2", "position": "The wāw is omitted for abbreviation, lightness, or conformity to the preceding fal-yadʿu.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says abbreviation; Bursawī and al-Ālūsī mention parallelism. {"id": "96:18/q04", "question": "How is the omitted wāw treated when recitation stops?", "turns_on": "Whether a stop follows written spelling, underlying form, or is discouraged.", "positions": [{"id": "96:18/q04/p1", "position": "Readers normally pause according to the written form, without restoring wāw.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī says all readers follow the rasm in four forms with omitted wāw before a still letter; his discussion of plural mīm uses sanadʿu as a comparable connected spelling.
